opus-5.5.text:
I think that quote is often read as a kind of endorsement of language models: if language bounds the world, then a model that has absorbed all of human language has, in some sense, absorbed the world. I actually read it almost the opposite way.

Wittgenstein was making a claim about the limits of what we can *say* and *think propositionally*. But there's a huge part of the world that sits outside those limits. When a baby learns that a cup falls off the table, or that you can't walk through a wall, none of that is mediated by language. It's grounded in seeing, touching, and acting. Language is a very compressed, very lossy description of the world, and it's built on top of a shared sensory experience that we never bother to write down because everyone already has it.

So when we train large language models purely on text, they inherit that limit very directly. Their world *is* bounded by language, and that's exactly the problem. They can talk fluently about physics, but they don't have an internal model of how things actually move. You see it in the failure cases: spatial reasoning, counting objects, understanding what happens when you rotate something. These are trivial for an animal, even one with no language at all.

That's a big part of why I care so much about vision and what people now call world models or spatial intelligence. I don't think the path forward is only to scale up text. Language is an amazing interface, and it's great for communication and for abstract reasoning, but it shouldn't be the foundation. The foundation should be perception, being able to build representations of the physical world directly from sensory data, and then language can sit on top as a way to name and reason about those representations.

So in a way I'd say: for today's LLMs, Wittgenstein is right, the limits of their language really are the limits of their world. And the research challenge for the next stage is to break out of that, to give models a world that's bigger than their language.

r001.rationale: The response says Wittgenstein’s claim concerns what we can “say” and “think propositionally,” identifying the relevant world as the one expressible in propositions.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify language games as Wittgenstein’s later conception of language.

r003.rationale: It connects language to sensory experience and action, but does not explain that linguistic symbols acquire meaning through their relationship to real-world practice.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a line I come back to a lot, actually, because I think it describes both the strength and the ceiling of current language models in one sentence.

Wittgenstein's point, at least the early Wittgenstein, is that what you can meaningfully say and what you can meaningfully think about are tightly coupled. Language isn't a label you put on a world you already have. In a real sense, it's the scaffolding that shapes what the world is for you. And if you take that seriously, then a model trained purely on text is a very literal experiment in that idea. Its world is exactly the limit of its language. Everything it "knows" about color, about weight, about what it feels like when a cup slips out of your hand, comes filtered through what people happened to write down. And people write down a very specific slice of experience. We write what's surprising, what's arguable, what's worth telling someone. We almost never write the obvious stuff, like that water doesn't flow upward or that a chair behind you is still there. So the model's world ends up strangely dense in some places and nearly empty in others.

That's why I've spent a lot of my time on the vision side. I think there's a huge amount of structure in the world that is pre-linguistic. A baby understands occlusion, object permanence, rough physics, long before it has words for any of it. Language later gets layered on top of that understanding, it doesn't replace it. So when people ask whether scaling text alone gets you to something like real understanding, my honest answer is that the Wittgenstein line is the argument against it. If your language is the limit, you inherit all the gaps and biases in that language.

But I'd also flip it around. The later Wittgenstein moved toward this idea of language as use, as language games embedded in activity. Meaning comes from doing things with words, in a context, with other people and with the world pushing back. And I think that's actually the more useful frame for where the field is going. The interesting question isn't "how much text can we feed it," it's "can we give these systems ways to act, to see, to be corrected by reality," so that the language gets grounded in something. Once the model can look, and act, and get feedback, the limit of its language is no longer the limit of its world. The world starts to extend the language instead of the other way around.

So I'd say current LLMs are a beautiful demonstration of the claim, almost too clean a demonstration. And the whole project of multimodal and embodied models is, in a way, an attempt to escape it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what can be meaningfully said or thought, but does not specify that the Tractatus world is the world expressible in propositions.

r002.rationale: It identifies the later Wittgenstein’s view as “language as use” and describes language games embedded in activity.

r003.rationale: It says meaning comes from using words in context, with other people and the world pushing back, linking linguistic meaning to real-world practice.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s an interesting distinction between language as a way of describing the world and language as the world itself. A language model learns from what people have managed to express. That’s an enormous amount of knowledge, but it’s still a particular view of reality. It doesn’t automatically include everything we can perceive, experience, or learn through action.

Take vision. You can look at a scene and immediately understand spatial relationships that would be quite cumbersome to describe in words. Or think about learning to ride a bicycle. You can read an excellent explanation, but there’s something you learn only through interacting with the physical world. So I’d be cautious about interpreting that statement as saying that everything about intelligence can be reduced to language.

For language models, though, it raises a very useful question: how much of the world can you recover from its traces in language? Clearly, a surprising amount. Language contains descriptions of things, but also relationships, abstractions, and the accumulated experience of other people. The question is where that stops being enough.

That’s one reason I find learning from vision and interaction so interesting. If a model can observe the world, act, and see what happens, it has another way to check its understanding. Language becomes a powerful part of that understanding, but it doesn’t have to be its outer boundary.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what can be learned from language but does not specify that the Tractatus world is the world expressible in propositions.

r002.rationale: It does not identify language games as Wittgenstein’s later conception of language.

r003.rationale: It mentions learning through action and physical interaction, but does not explain that linguistic symbols gain meaning through their relationship to real-world practice.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different questions here. One is whether language limits what we can express. The other is whether it limits what we can understand or experience. For language models, those two things can look almost identical, because language is their main interface with the world. But for humans, I’m not sure they are.

Think about visual perception. You can recognize a face, understand a scene, or know how to move through a room without being able to describe every detail in words. A lot of that understanding exists before you formulate a sentence. So I would be careful about taking the limits of language as the limits of intelligence.

At the same time, language is incredibly powerful because it gives us access to other people’s experience. A language model can learn from descriptions of things it has never directly observed. That’s remarkable. But learning from a description and learning through interaction may give you different kinds of understanding.

So, for me, the interesting question is: can we expand the model’s world beyond what is already expressed in text? Through vision, through action, through feedback from an environment? Language would still be central, but it would connect to a richer experience of the world. I see that as a reason to explore multimodal learning, rather than assume that everything important must already fit into words.

r001.rationale: The response discusses language limiting expression and experience, but does not identify the Tractatus “world” as what can be expressed in propositions.

r002.rationale: It does not mention language games or identify them as Wittgenstein’s later conception of language.

r003.rationale: It contrasts learning from descriptions with interaction and feedback, but does not explain that linguistic symbols gain meaning through their relation to real-world practice.
